title: Transfer pricing basics for cross-border transaction disputes
p1:
A company can make a profit and still face a tax dispute across borders.

Why? The price charged between related companies in different countries may become the real battlefield.
p2:
Many people think transfer pricing is about simply setting prices. The surprising part is that tax authorities often question whether those prices are fair, not whether a business transaction happened.

For example, a parent company selling services to its overseas subsidiary must show that the price is similar to what independent companies would agree on.
p3:
This idea is called the “arm’s length principle” — treating related businesses as if they were unrelated partners. When countries disagree on whether a price is reasonable, disputes can lead to extra taxes, penalties, and lengthy negotiations.

A practical takeaway: businesses involved in international transactions should keep clear records showing how prices were decided before a dispute begins.
conclusion: Have you ever wondered how companies prove that a cross-border transaction price is fair when tax authorities challenge it?
